scenario_stem:
CarePlus Pharmacies is a regional pharmacy chain of 6 branches in Country X, employing 38 pharmacists and assistants. The business generated $720,000 in revenue last year and holds an 8% share of the local prescription market. Repeat prescription sales account for 70% of turnover. Following the introduction of a new home-delivery prescription service for elderly customers, the marketing director must promote it to 9,000 regular patients aged over 65.

The branch manager can spend $6,000 on informative advertising through newspaper notices and local radio announcements explaining how the delivery service works, its $3 delivery charge and the sign-up process. Alternatively, the same $6,000 could fund persuasive advertising using emotional television commercials showing grandparents receiving medicines at home. The board wants strong sign-up numbers within 3 months.

questions.model_answer: Advertising that provides factual information to consumers about a product, such as its features, price, availability or how to use it [2].

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Informative advertising provides the factual details customers need before adopting an unfamiliar service [k], such as the $3 delivery charge and sign-up process for elderly patients aged over 65 [app]. Reason 2: It suits older audiences who rely on local newspapers and radio [k], helping CarePlus reach its 9,000 regular patients across 6 branches in Country X [app].

Benefit 2: These media cost much less per placement than television [k], stretching the limited $6,000 budget further than TV commercials would [app], allowing the campaign to run longer and hold local awareness until the 3-month deadline [an].

However, persuasive advertising creates emotional impact [k], showing grandparents receiving medicines at home to elderly viewers across Country X [app], building stronger brand warmth and reaching households beyond the current 8% market share [an]. Overall, informative advertising is better here because the service is new and simple to explain [eval], so factual clarity will drive sign-ups within the 3-month window more reliably than emotional appeals [eval].

scenario_stem:
Aurora Cosmetics is a private limited company that has manufactured natural skincare for 5 years, employing 24 staff at its factory in Country X. Annual revenue reached $1.4 million last year, with its new anti-ageing face cream accounting for $380,000 of sales across 11 pharmacy chains. Its loyal customers cite natural ingredients as the main purchase reason, yet growth of the cream has slowed sharply this year. The marketing team is preparing the relaunch campaign, backed by a $90,000 promotional budget.

The marketing manager must choose between persuasive advertising and informative advertising. Persuasive television commercials featuring a well-known celebrity would cost $60,000 and reach 1.2 million viewers per week. Continuing the previous informative approach would list ingredients and clinical test results in glossy magazines, at $12,000 per issue, leaving budget for several insertions.

Reason 2: It can make the brand memorable quickly [k], and with 1.2 million weekly viewers reachable on television the relaunch would be seen far beyond the 11 pharmacy chains already stocking the cream [app].

Disadvantage 2: It can struggle to differentiate the brand in a crowded skincare market [k], since rival firms also advertise in the same magazines their target readers see [app], meaning Aurora's $90,000 budget may deliver weaker awareness and slower sales growth [an].

scenario_stem:
BrightBuy Supermarkets operates 14 stores across Country X, employing 420 workers and generating $9.6 million in annual revenue. The weekly marketing budget is $18,000. Cereal is a key traffic-driving aisle for weekly family grocery shops and BrightBuy wants to win it back from rivals. To lift slow cereal sales, currently 300 boxes per store per week and 25% below target, the marketing manager must choose between two sales promotions for the own-brand cornflakes range.

Option 1 is BOGOF (buy one, get one free) on own-brand cornflakes, costing an estimated $7,500 per week and expected to double unit sales. Option 2 is a 20% price reduction from $4.00 to $3.20 per box, costing around $5,800 per week with only modest sales growth expected. The board wants higher sales volume while protecting profit margins.

questions.question_text: Define 'sales promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Short-term incentives designed to encourage customers to purchase a product, such as price reductions, BOGOF offers, competitions or free gifts [2].

knowledge_max_2: short-term incentives to encourage product purchase

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why BrightBuy Supermarkets might use sales promotion to increase breakfast cereal sales.

Reason 2: Promotions can pull customers away from rival supermarkets [k], which matters when BrightBuy generates $9.6 million in revenue and wants to protect its share of household grocery spending [app].

Disadvantage 2: Customers may become conditioned to expect free offers [k], damaging sales of regular-priced lines once the $7,500 weekly promotion ends [app], leaving the 25% shortfall to reappear without continual discounting [an].

However, a 20% price reduction from $4.00 to $3.20 costs only $5,800 per week [k], is simpler to operate on shelf and keeps customers paying something for every box [app], preserving more margin than giving a full box away [an]. Overall, BOGOF is the better promotion because the board's key objective is restoring sales volume, and the extra $1,700 per week is justified if double-unit sales are achieved [eval], though a shorter trial period would limit the conditioned-expectation risk [eval].

scenario_stem:
Crunchy Harvest Snacks is a partnership producing baked oat bars stocked by 8 supermarket chains in Country X. It employs 16 workers and sales reached $640,000 last year. Early tasting trials with 300 shoppers scored the new flavour 4.5 out of 5, above the partnership's launch threshold. To launch a new peanut-butter oat bar the partners have a $15,000 promotional budget and must choose between two sales promotions.

Option 1 is free samples: staff handing out 10,000 sample bars at store entrances over 4 weekends. Option 2 is a gift promotion: a free reusable lunchbox with every 6-bar multipack, costing $9,000 for 5,000 lunchboxes. The partners expect samples to convert at a 20% trial-to-purchase rate, while lunchbox multipacks should lift multipack sales by 30% during the 6-week campaign.

Reason 2: They can convert trial into repeat purchase [k], and at an expected 20% trial-to-purchase rate on 10,000 samples the partners could gain around 2,000 new buyers [app].

However, the lunchbox gift with the 6-bar multipack should lift multipack sales by 30% during the 6-week campaign [k], appealing to family shoppers already buying Crunchy Harvest products across the 8 supermarket chains [app], which may lift immediate revenue more than small samples [an]. scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Titan Industrial Tools is a private limited company manufacturing heavy-duty pressure washers for garages and farms. It employs 45 workers at one factory in Country X and generated $3.8 million in revenue last year. Existing dealer satisfaction stands at 92%, but brand awareness remains low outside its present dealer network. Each TX-900 washer sells for $2,500 and dealer contracts average $40,000 per year.

The sales director must decide how to launch the new TX-900. Option 1 is personal selling: hiring 6 commission-paid sales representatives to visit garages, give demonstrations and negotiate contracts, costing $120,000 in salaries and travel for 12 months. Option 2 is advertising in national trade magazines and on industry websites, costing $45,000 for a one-year campaign reaching an estimated 30,000 potential business buyers.

Reason 2: Personal contact lets the business build long-term relationships and negotiate large orders [k], which fits dealer contracts averaging $40,000 a year and washers retailing at $2,500 [app].

Disadvantage 2: Reach is limited by the number of visits representatives can make [k], so the TX-900 could miss the 30,000 potential business buyers exposed to a $45,000 magazine and website campaign [app], slowing industry-wide awareness of the new model [an].

However, advertising in trade magazines and on industry websites for $45,000 reaches an estimated 30,000 potential business buyers at a fraction of the $120,000 personal selling cost [k], creating broad awareness of the TX-900 across the industry within a single campaign [app], feeding the sales pipeline before representatives visit [an]. Option 1 is a public relations offensive: hosting a charity dinner for 150 local business leaders and travel journalists with a press release offering the hotel's response, costing $12,000. scenario_stem:
PureWeight Foods is a private limited company producing 'LeanLine' weight-loss biscuits promoted as 'clinically proven to burn belly fat'. It employs 60 workers, sales reached $1.8 million last year, and Trading Standards has flagged the pack claim as potentially misleading promotion. A routine inspection also found 500g packets averaging only 450g, breaching weights and measures law.

The managing director must choose between two options. Option 1 is to withdraw all LeanLine stock, reprint packaging with revised claims and recalibrate the filling machinery at a cost of $80,000, halting the promotion for 2 months. Option 2 is to continue selling current stock with the existing promotion unchanged and contest the ruling, risking fines and compensation claims with legal costs estimated at $25,000, but protecting $600,000 of near-term sales.

questions.question_text: Define 'misleading promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Promotion that gives consumers a false or deceptive impression about a product, such as untrue claims about what it can do, which consumer protection law prohibits [2].

Control 2: Misleading promotion law forbids untrue or unproven product claims [k], so the claim that LeanLine is 'clinically proven to burn belly fat' is unlawful unless the company holds genuine clinical evidence [app].
